title: Reverse Linked List
statement:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head.

Reuse the existing nodes by changing their `next` pointers — don't build a new list. The list may be empty, in which case `head` is `null` and you should return `null`.

target.note: the benchmark time includes building the input list, which is also linear

hints: When you flip a node's next pointer to point backwards, what do you lose, and what do you need to have saved first?
Walk the list with two pointers: prev (the already-reversed part) and cur (the rest). Before pointing cur.next at prev, save cur.next in a temporary.
Start with prev = null, cur = head. Loop while cur != null: next = cur.next; cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = next. When the loop ends, prev is the new head.
followups: Write it recursively. What's the space cost, and when would that matter?
Reverse only the nodes between positions left and right, in one pass.
Reverse the list in groups of k nodes.
explain: Iterate with prev = null and cur = head. At each node, save next = cur.next, point cur.next back at prev, then advance both pointers (prev = cur, cur = next). The invariant is that prev heads a fully reversed list of the nodes visited so far, while cur heads the untouched rest; when cur is null, prev is the answer. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) extra space, and the empty and single-node lists need no special case. The recursive version — reverse head.next, then set head.next.next = head and head.next = null — is elegant but uses O(n) stack, which can overflow on a long list in Java's default thread stack.
